user_query: What did DRCR.net Protocol T compare in diabetic retinopathy / DME research?
draft_answer: DRCR.net Protocol T was a significant study in diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema (DME) research that compared the efficacy of three anti-VEGF agents: aflibercept, bevacizumab, and ranibizumab. This randomized trial aimed to evaluate the visual outcomes and safety profiles of these treatments in patients with DME. The study provided insights into the comparative effectiveness of these drugs, which are commonly used in clinical practice for managing DME [2]. The trial's findings have been influential in guiding treatment decisions and optimizing patient care in diabetic eye disease [2].

claims.claim_text: DRCR.net Protocol T compared aflibercept, bevacizumab, and ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema.

chunks.document_content: Introduction new therapeutic targets and developing more effica­ cious treatment strategies have become particularly urgent. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), as one of the most com­ mon microvascular complications of diabetes, affects approximately 34.6% of individuals living with dia­ betes, with 30% progressing to varying degrees of vis­ ual impairment (Wang et al., 2024). The pathological characteristics primarily include capillary degener­ ation, loss of pericytes, and vessel leakage (Liu et al., 2023). At present, the therapeutic strategies for DR mainly focus on systemic treatment, vitrectomy, ret­ inal photocoagulation, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF inhibitors (Yamato et al., 2024). While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Thus, exploring As intrinsic resident immune cells of the retina, microglia maintain homeostatic distribution under physiological conditions and participate in the dynamic equilibrium of the retinal microenvironment by constantly surveilling the local microenvironment, clearing metabolic waste, and stabilizing synaptic structures (Guo et al., 2022). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a. chunks.document_content: Published: October 16, 2026 The level of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is commonly used to characterize ocular microvascular complications of diabetes, the leading cause of preventable blindness amongst working-aged people [1]. Shorter durations of diabetes, improved glycemic control, and lower blood pressure and lipid levels are implicated in reducing the risk for development and progression of DR [2]. A review of prior research [3] identified studies focused on prevalence, incidence and progression of DR and the risk factors associated with them. However, regression (or improvement) of DR is less frequently studied or is a secondary focus. Available studies on regression (Table 1) suggest it is more likely to occur in very mild nonproliferative DR (NPDR) [6,19], particularly for younger patients with hemo­ globin A1c (HbA1c) levels close to normal and shorter diabetes duration [11,13,16]. Generally, the literature addressing regression focused on improvements in risk factors known to be associated with progression of DR. However, one publication [8] suggested that the formation of microaneurysms (MAs), a characteristic lesion for mild NPDR, was independent of glycemic control and other medical factors that affect more advanced levels of DR. Sterphanie The primary aim of this study was to investigate the occurrence of DR regression in teleophthalmology patients with initially very mild NPDR or mild NPDR. Rates of no change or stability and any progression were also determined for comparison pur­ poses. A secondary aim was to examine the association of diabetes therapy, diabetes duration, and HbA1c with regression occurrence. Prior results on this study cohort [20,21] demonstrated prevalence of any DR, any DME, and sight-threatening disease was 28.6%, 3.0%, and 3.0%. Of patients with no DR in 2015, 18.0% had mild NPDR or worse in 2016-2019, and 0.1% had PDR. Of patients with mild NPDR in 2015, 27.2% progressed to moderate NPDR or worse in 2016-2019, and 2.3% progressed to severe NPDR or worse.

chunks.document_content: Materials and methods Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has long been assessed primarily as a microangiopathy. However, recent studies have proposed the con-cept of diabetic retinal disease (DRD), which recognizes that retinal pathology involves not only the vascular system but also neural and glial cells and their interactions within the neurovascular unit (2, 3). This concept has increased interest in preclinical and early clinical signs of DRD to better understand the mechanisms and timing of disease onset (2). Both basic and clinical studies have demonstrated subtle but clear functional and structural changes in retinal neural tissue in diabetes (4-8). To analyze these early changes, we have been studying diabetic eyes at a stage before visible macular changes are detectable on fundus photographs and before the development of secondary changes associated with PDR and/or exudative fluid in DME (9, 10). However, their associations with systemic biomarkers have not yet been addressed, although diabetic complications tend to be associated not only with hyperglycemia but also with broader systemic metabolic alterations. Participants Non-invasive ocular imaging systems, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA), can detect subtle changes at the micrometer scale and are now widely used in clinical practice. OCT enables measurement not only of the thick-ness of the neural retinal layers but also of photoreceptor outer segment (PROS) length. Length of the PROS, where visual pigments are concentrated and act as light receptors, has been reported to be reduced in eyes with diabetes than in control (10), and as a marker of photoreceptor condition in eyes at high risk of age-related macular degeneration (11, 12). The volume of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a highly metabolic single-cell layer essential for photoreceptor maintenance, can also be measured on OCT images. Eye examinations The patients underwent ophthalmic examinations, including measurement of BCVA, intraocular pressure (IOP), and axial length, and acquisition of fundus photographs (California, Optos, Inc., MA), sectional and three-dimensional spectral-domain OCT images (Spectralis OCT, Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Dossenheim, Germany), and 3 x 3 mm OCT angiography (OCTA) (OCT HS-100; Canon, Inc., Tokyo, Japan) images. chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Martina Tomic ́, Merkur University Hospital, Croatia RECEIVED 07 August 2026 REVISED 27 September 2026 ACCEPTED 29 September 2026 PUBLISHED 09 October 2026 Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices Zixuan Wang 1, Xuwei Liu 2, Ming Yang 3, Guanchi Yan 3, Xuechun Fan 1, Jing Yu 3, Jinyue Zhao 3, Yingjing Shi 4* and Xi Chen 3* 1College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 2School of Environment and Energy, Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture, Beijing, China, 3The Affiliated Hospital to Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 4Changchun Disabled Persons Rehabilitation Center, Changchun, China CITATION Wang Z, Liu X, Yang M, Yan G, Fan X, Yu J, Zhao J, Shi Y and Chen X (2026) Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices. Front. Endocrinol. 17:1961622. doi: 10.3389/fendo.XXX-XXX-XXXX Background: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent and sight-threatening ocular complication of diabetes, and one of the leading causes of vision loss and blindness among the working-age population worldwide. Driven by a growing understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying DR, treatment strategies have evolved from a sole focus on glycemic control to comprehensive, multi-targeted, and multimodal therapies. This study systematically summarizes the characteristics of current clinical trials focused on DR treatment and evaluates the employed research methodologies. The aim of this review is to explore methodological trends in specific domains, with the hope that such insights may inform future efforts to optimize trial design and improve trial quality. Methods: This study followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) were retrieved. In addition, clinical trials indexed in PubMed from July 23, 2016 to July 23, 2026 were retrieved. Data from the included studies were extracted and presented in tabular form. Results: Clinical research targeting DR has expanded rapidly, reflecting a shift toward diverse interventions like anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor(anti-VEGF) drugs, laser treatments, and combined therapies. However, several methodological limitations were noted in the included studies, including the failure to specify diabetes type in over half of the cases, a predominance of small-sample trials, inconsistent reporting of intervention duration, and limited implementation of blinding due to practical constraints in ophthalmic interventions. chunks.document_name: pubmed_42898801_PMC13678296_From validation to public health impact_ implementing equita.pdf
chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS *CORRESPONDENCE Jing Chen RECEIVED 24 August 2026 REVISED 21 September 2026 ACCEPTED 25 September 2026 PUBLISHED 05 October 2026 Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a preventable cause of vision loss as diabetes prevalence rises worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled retinal screening has progressed from retrospective validation to prospective and real-world deployment, with recent reviews showing high diagnostic performance across fundus photography, smartphone-based systems, and autonomous platforms. Yet diagnostic accuracy alone does not ensure public health benefit. Population impact can be lost when eligible people are not reached, images are ungradable, results are delayed, referrals are incomplete, treatment capacity is insufficient, or disadvantaged groups face financial, geographic, or digital barriers. Unlike reviews centered mainly on diagnostic accuracy or economic performance, this Mini Review reframes AI-enabled DR screening as a population-health intervention spanning detection through completion of effective eye care. We synthesize evidence on diagnostic validity, implementation, economics, referral completion, care cascades, patient-centered outcomes, equity, and governance. We argue that effectiveness and cost-effectiveness are properties of the complete screening-to-treatment pathway, not the algorithm alone, and propose a four-domain framework encompassing technical validity, service integration, population impact, and equity and sustainability. Future research should prioritize comparative implementation studies and outcome sets that capture screening reach, gradability, referral completion, treatment initiation, time to treatment, avoidable vision loss, vision-related quality of life, acceptability, costs, and subgroup equity. The policy question is no longer whether AI can detect DR, but whether health systems can translate automated detection into equitable completion of effective eye care at scale. CITATION Chen J and Chen B (2026) From validation to public health impact: implementing equitable AI-enabled diabetic retinopathy screening. Front. Public Health 14:1976572. doi: 10.3389/fpubh.XXX-XXX-XXXX COPYRIGHT © 2026 Chen and Chen. KEYWORDS artificial intelligence, diabetic retinopathy, health equity, implementation science, public health, quality of life, referral completion, screening Introduction Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a common microvascular complication of diabetes and a preventable cause of vision loss when sight-threatening disease is detected and treated early (1). The public health challenge is expanding as diabetes prevalence rises: the International Diabetes Federation estimates that 589 million adults were living with diabetes in 2024, with projections approaching 853 million by 2050 (2). Updated global estimates suggest that more than 100 million adults already have DR, and the number is expected to increase substantially by 2045 (3). In this context, screening is not simply an ophthalmic service; it is a population-level strategy that links chronic disease management, primary care, imaging infrastructure, referral pathways, and timely treatment (4).

chunks.document_content: 1 Introduction readability have been reported in myopia, retinal disease, and DR-related patient-information contexts (11-14). Nevertheless, many existing evaluations have focused primarily on factual cor­ rectness, readability, or overall response quality, and relatively few have integrated safety, patient-centered communication, struc­ tured information-quality measures, transparency, and readability within a single DR-focused evaluation. Consequently, existing evidence does not fully characterize how publicly accessible LLM interfaces perform across the multiple dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR education. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most common microvas­ cular complications of diabetes and remains a leading cause of pre­ ventable vision impairment among working-age adults worldwide. A global meta-analysis estimated that 22.3% of individuals with diabetes have DR and 6.2% have vision-threatening DR, corresponding to approximately 103 million affected adults in 2020 and a projected increase to 160 million by 2045 (1). Much of the vision loss associated with DR is potentially preventable through timely retinal screening, systemic risk-factor control, appropriate referral, and evidence-based treatment (2, 3). However, early DR is frequently asymptomatic, and the effectiveness of prevention depends partly on whether individuals understand screening recommendations, attend follow-up examina­ tions, and seek timely care after abnormal findings or new visual symptoms. People living with diabetes therefore require accessible and understandable health education regarding screening intervals, warn­ ing symptoms, treatment options, pregnancy-related risks, and long-term self-management. To address this gap, we conducted a CHART-aligned comparative evaluation of six widely accessible LLM interfaces-ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity-using 50 stan­ dardized patient-oriented DR questions (15). Unlike evaluations cen­ tered on a narrower set of outcomes, the present study combined guideline-based Safety and Accuracy assessment with Empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, Global Quality Score, and six readability metrics. This multidimensional, time-stamped design was intended to characterize how publicly accessible interfaces perform across the informational, communicative, safety, transpar­ ency, and readability dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR educa­ tion. Rather than establishing a permanent model ranking, the study identifies strengths, trade-offs, and areas that warrant evaluation before LLM-generated information is incorporated into routine patient education. Patients increasingly seek health information online, and con­ versational artificial intelligence systems are becoming readily accessible sources of patient-facing medical information (4). Large language models (LLMs) are emerging not only as question-answering technologies but also as digital health information sources and population-facing health communication channels. Their immediate and conversational responses may help address unmet information needs, particularly for chronic conditions that require repeated health education. However, LLM-generated information may also influence how users understand disease risk, interpret symptoms, and make decisions about screening and care-seeking. Responses that provide inaccurate screening inter­ vals, inadequate urgent-care advice, unrealistic treatment expecta­ tions, or unclear boundaries between AI-assisted screening and professional evaluation could contribute to delayed or inappropri­ ate care. Information that is technically accurate but excessively difficult to read may also be inaccessible to individuals with lim­ ited health literacy. This concern is particularly relevant because ophthalmic patient-education materials frequently exceed recom­ mended readability levels (5, 6).

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), as one of the most com­ mon microvascular complications of diabetes, affects approximately 34.6% of individuals living with dia­ betes, with 30% progressing to varying degrees of vis­ ual impairment (Wang et al., 2024). The pathological characteristics primarily include capillary degener­ ation, loss of pericytes, and vessel leakage (Liu et al., 2023). At present, the therapeutic strategies for DR mainly focus on systemic treatment, vitrectomy, ret­ inal photocoagulation, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF inhibitors (Yamato et al., 2024). While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a. chunks.document_name: pubmed_42921263_PMC13692711_Early changes in the central vision and the macula in diabet.pdf
chunks.document_content: Materials and methods Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has long been assessed primarily as a microangiopathy. However, recent studies have proposed the con-cept of diabetic retinal disease (DRD), which recognizes that retinal pathology involves not only the vascular system but also neural and glial cells and their interactions within the neurovascular unit (2, 3). This concept has increased interest in preclinical and early clinical signs of DRD to better understand the mechanisms and timing of disease onset (2). Both basic and clinical studies have demonstrated subtle but clear functional and structural changes in retinal neural tissue in diabetes (4-8). To analyze these early changes, we have been studying diabetic eyes at a stage before visible macular changes are detectable on fundus photographs and before the development of secondary changes associated with PDR and/or exudative fluid in DME (9, 10). However, their associations with systemic biomarkers have not yet been addressed, although diabetic complications tend to be associated not only with hyperglycemia but also with broader systemic metabolic alterations. Participants Non-invasive ocular imaging systems, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA), can detect subtle changes at the micrometer scale and are now widely used in clinical practice. OCT enables measurement not only of the thick-ness of the neural retinal layers but also of photoreceptor outer segment (PROS) length. Length of the PROS, where visual pigments are concentrated and act as light receptors, has been reported to be reduced in eyes with diabetes than in control (10), and as a marker of photoreceptor condition in eyes at high risk of age-related macular degeneration (11, 12). The volume of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a highly metabolic single-cell layer essential for photoreceptor maintenance, can also be measured on OCT images. Eye examinations The patients underwent ophthalmic examinations, including measurement of BCVA, intraocular pressure (IOP), and axial length, and acquisition of fundus photographs (California, Optos, Inc., MA), sectional and three-dimensional spectral-domain OCT images (Spectralis OCT, Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Dossenheim, Germany), and 3 x 3 mm OCT angiography (OCTA) (OCT HS-100; Canon, Inc., Tokyo, Japan) images. chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Martina Tomic ́, Merkur University Hospital, Croatia RECEIVED 07 August 2026 REVISED 27 September 2026 ACCEPTED 29 September 2026 PUBLISHED 09 October 2026 Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices Zixuan Wang 1, Xuwei Liu 2, Ming Yang 3, Guanchi Yan 3, Xuechun Fan 1, Jing Yu 3, Jinyue Zhao 3, Yingjing Shi 4* and Xi Chen 3* 1College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 2School of Environment and Energy, Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture, Beijing, China, 3The Affiliated Hospital to Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 4Changchun Disabled Persons Rehabilitation Center, Changchun, China CITATION Wang Z, Liu X, Yang M, Yan G, Fan X, Yu J, Zhao J, Shi Y and Chen X (2026) Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices. Front. Endocrinol. 17:1961622. doi: 10.3389/fendo.XXX-XXX-XXXX Background: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent and sight-threatening ocular complication of diabetes, and one of the leading causes of vision loss and blindness among the working-age population worldwide. Driven by a growing understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying DR, treatment strategies have evolved from a sole focus on glycemic control to comprehensive, multi-targeted, and multimodal therapies. This study systematically summarizes the characteristics of current clinical trials focused on DR treatment and evaluates the employed research methodologies. The aim of this review is to explore methodological trends in specific domains, with the hope that such insights may inform future efforts to optimize trial design and improve trial quality. Methods: This study followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) were retrieved. In addition, clinical trials indexed in PubMed from July 23, 2016 to July 23, 2026 were retrieved. Data from the included studies were extracted and presented in tabular form. Results: Clinical research targeting DR has expanded rapidly, reflecting a shift toward diverse interventions like anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor(anti-VEGF) drugs, laser treatments, and combined therapies. However, several methodological limitations were noted in the included studies, including the failure to specify diabetes type in over half of the cases, a predominance of small-sample trials, inconsistent reporting of intervention duration, and limited implementation of blinding due to practical constraints in ophthalmic interventions. chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS *CORRESPONDENCE Jing Chen RECEIVED 24 August 2026 REVISED 21 September 2026 ACCEPTED 25 September 2026 PUBLISHED 05 October 2026 Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a preventable cause of vision loss as diabetes prevalence rises worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled retinal screening has progressed from retrospective validation to prospective and real-world deployment, with recent reviews showing high diagnostic performance across fundus photography, smartphone-based systems, and autonomous platforms. Yet diagnostic accuracy alone does not ensure public health benefit. Population impact can be lost when eligible people are not reached, images are ungradable, results are delayed, referrals are incomplete, treatment capacity is insufficient, or disadvantaged groups face financial, geographic, or digital barriers. Unlike reviews centered mainly on diagnostic accuracy or economic performance, this Mini Review reframes AI-enabled DR screening as a population-health intervention spanning detection through completion of effective eye care. We synthesize evidence on diagnostic validity, implementation, economics, referral completion, care cascades, patient-centered outcomes, equity, and governance. We argue that effectiveness and cost-effectiveness are properties of the complete screening-to-treatment pathway, not the algorithm alone, and propose a four-domain framework encompassing technical validity, service integration, population impact, and equity and sustainability. Future research should prioritize comparative implementation studies and outcome sets that capture screening reach, gradability, referral completion, treatment initiation, time to treatment, avoidable vision loss, vision-related quality of life, acceptability, costs, and subgroup equity. The policy question is no longer whether AI can detect DR, but whether health systems can translate automated detection into equitable completion of effective eye care at scale. CITATION Chen J and Chen B (2026) From validation to public health impact: implementing equitable AI-enabled diabetic retinopathy screening. Front. KEYWORDS artificial intelligence, diabetic retinopathy, health equity, implementation science, public health, quality of life, referral completion, screening Introduction Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a common microvascular complication of diabetes and a preventable cause of vision loss when sight-threatening disease is detected and treated early (1). The public health challenge is expanding as diabetes prevalence rises: the International Diabetes Federation estimates that 589 million adults were living with diabetes in 2024, with projections approaching 853 million by 2050 (2). Updated global estimates suggest that more than 100 million adults already have DR, and the number is expected to increase substantially by 2045 (3). In this context, screening is not simply an ophthalmic service; it is a population-level strategy that links chronic disease management, primary care, imaging infrastructure, referral pathways, and timely treatment (4).

chunks.document_content: 1 Introduction readability have been reported in myopia, retinal disease, and DR-related patient-information contexts (11-14). Nevertheless, many existing evaluations have focused primarily on factual cor­ rectness, readability, or overall response quality, and relatively few have integrated safety, patient-centered communication, struc­ tured information-quality measures, transparency, and readability within a single DR-focused evaluation. Consequently, existing evidence does not fully characterize how publicly accessible LLM interfaces perform across the multiple dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR education. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most common microvas­ cular complications of diabetes and remains a leading cause of pre­ ventable vision impairment among working-age adults worldwide. A global meta-analysis estimated that 22.3% of individuals with diabetes have DR and 6.2% have vision-threatening DR, corresponding to approximately 103 million affected adults in 2020 and a projected increase to 160 million by 2045 (1). Much of the vision loss associated with DR is potentially preventable through timely retinal screening, systemic risk-factor control, appropriate referral, and evidence-based treatment (2, 3). However, early DR is frequently asymptomatic, and the effectiveness of prevention depends partly on whether individuals understand screening recommendations, attend follow-up examina­ tions, and seek timely care after abnormal findings or new visual symptoms. People living with diabetes therefore require accessible and understandable health education regarding screening intervals, warn­ ing symptoms, treatment options, pregnancy-related risks, and long-term self-management. To address this gap, we conducted a CHART-aligned comparative evaluation of six widely accessible LLM interfaces-ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity-using 50 stan­ dardized patient-oriented DR questions (15). Unlike evaluations cen­ tered on a narrower set of outcomes, the present study combined guideline-based Safety and Accuracy assessment with Empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, Global Quality Score, and six readability metrics. This multidimensional, time-stamped design was intended to characterize how publicly accessible interfaces perform across the informational, communicative, safety, transpar­ ency, and readability dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR educa­ tion. Rather than establishing a permanent model ranking, the study identifies strengths, trade-offs, and areas that warrant evaluation before LLM-generated information is incorporated into routine patient education. Patients increasingly seek health information online, and con­ versational artificial intelligence systems are becoming readily accessible sources of patient-facing medical information (4). Large language models (LLMs) are emerging not only as question-answering technologies but also as digital health information sources and population-facing health communication channels. Their immediate and conversational responses may help address unmet information needs, particularly for chronic conditions that require repeated health education. However, LLM-generated information may also influence how users understand disease risk, interpret symptoms, and make decisions about screening and care-seeking. Responses that provide inaccurate screening inter­ vals, inadequate urgent-care advice, unrealistic treatment expecta­ tions, or unclear boundaries between AI-assisted screening and professional evaluation could contribute to delayed or inappropri­ ate care. Information that is technically accurate but excessively difficult to read may also be inaccessible to individuals with lim­ ited health literacy. This concern is particularly relevant because ophthalmic patient-education materials frequently exceed recom­ mended readability levels (5, 6).
